content: The term multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) refers to a group of distinct syndromes characterized by the presence of tumors in endocrine glands. Each syndrome has its own unique pattern of tumor development. In some cases, these tumors are malignant, while in others, they are benign. Additionally, benign or malignant tumors of non-endocrine tissues may also occur as part of these tumor syndromes. MEN syndromes are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, meaning that a single copy of the mutated gene from an affected parent is sufficient to cause the disorder in offspring. The percentages mentioned in comparisons refer to the proportion of individuals with a specific type of MEN who develop a particular type of neoplasia. For example, a certain percentage of patients with MEN1 may develop gastrinomas. MEN syndromes are also associated with other conditions, such as Von Hippel-Lindau disease and Carney complex. Surgical intervention is the cornerstone of treatment for tumors associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia. Surgery is typically employed to remove the tumors and manage the associated symptoms.
